sections.h2: What must a Bloomington seller do before listing a house?
sections.html:
Before you list, show or sell a house in Bloomington, the city requires a Time-of-Sale housing inspection and a filed evaluation report. The rule covers single and two-family dwellings, condominiums, townhouses and mobile homes, and it applies to private sales as well, including a sale to a family member that is never listed. Multi-family rental buildings of four or more units are left out.

This requirement is the biggest difference between selling here and selling in most Minnesota suburbs, so it shapes the whole timeline. Cash buyers purchase as-is, but the city's inspection step still applies to the sale. The rest of this page walks through what the inspection costs, what it can force you to fix and who can take on a hazard.

sections.h2: How does the Bloomington Time-of-Sale inspection work?
sections.html:
The owner or listing agent schedules the inspection with the city's Building and Inspections Division at 952-563-8930 or through an online request form, and the evaluator needs about 120 minutes on site. The fee is $250, which includes the energy disclosure and any re-inspections, plus a service fee of $1.95 for an e-check or 2.95 percent for a card. If you cancel before a site visit, the city offers a refund of up to 50 percent within 60 days of your request.

  • The evaluator examines visible structure, heating, electrical and plumbing, and accessible attics and crawl spaces, and does not take anything apart.
  • The report does not cover lead paint, radon or asbestos, and it does not guarantee the home.
  • The report must be displayed at the house and given to the buyer before or at sale, and a copy must reach the city within 7 calendar days.
  • The report and the Certificate of Compliance are good for one year and only for the owner named on them.

Since April 2022 the inspection has included an energy disclosure covering the heating and cooling system, water heater, insulation and windows, and the city says no energy upgrades are required of the seller.

sections.h2: What counts as an immediate hazard, and who pays to fix it?
sections.html:
Only nine categories of defect must be corrected, and the seller is responsible unless the buyer agrees in writing to take them over. The city lists them as unsafe heating systems, unsafe water heaters, dangerous electrical conditions, unsanitary plumbing, structures unable to carry their loads, roofs, walls and foundations that are not weather tight, abandoned fuel tanks, unsanitary refuse or infestation, and missing or non-working smoke detectors.

Other defects are noted in the report but do not have to be repaired. If hazards are found, a re-inspection by a city inspector is required before the house can be occupied, and the owner or contractor must pull any permits. A buyer who is willing to take the hazards must get the city's written consent by signing a Hazard Correction/Responsibility form, which is currently handled through DocuSign by calling the same 952-563-8930 line. The Certificate of Compliance is typically required at closing.

sections.h2: Which sales are exempt from the Bloomington inspection?
sections.html:
Five kinds of transfer are exempt, but you must still call the city to say which exemption you are using. They are a newly built dwelling transferred to its first owner, a multiple dwelling already licensed as rental, a sale to a public body, a sale for demolition, and a sale by a sheriff or other court officer. The last exemption does not cover a sale by someone appointed by a probate court, which matters for heirs selling an inherited Bloomington house.

If your sale does not fit an exemption, plan for the inspection and the report date before you set a closing. Check any open work permits as well, because the owner or contractor must obtain the necessary permits and the dwelling is subject to re-inspection of open permits before occupancy.

sections.h2: What is Bloomington like, and who shops for homes here?
sections.html:
Bloomington is the largest suburb in the Twin Cities, with 89,034 people, 10 miles south of downtown Minneapolis on the north bank of the Minnesota River. It was settled in 1843, the Town of Bloomington was incorporated on May 11, 1858, and it became a city on November 8, 1960. The postwar housing boom filled in much of the street grid you see today.

Interstate 35W divides the city informally. West Bloomington is mostly residential with newer housing, while East Bloomington has more industry, retail and the less expensive housing. Highway 77 (Cedar Avenue), Highway 169 and Interstate 494 frame the rest of the map, and the Metro Blue Line light rail runs from the Mall of America to downtown Minneapolis and both airport terminals.

The employer base is strong. Mall of America tenants are the largest group, with Dayforce, Donaldson, Great Clips, HealthPartners and Toro headquartered here. ISD 271 runs fifteen public schools, with John F. Kennedy High School in the east and Thomas Jefferson High School in the west, and the attendance line runs near France and Xerxes Avenues. A buyer will ask which side of that line you are on.

sections.h2: Which city fees and bills should a seller check before closing?
sections.html:
Before closing, call the city to find out whether anything is owed on the property, because outstanding items are easier to clear before the title company asks. The city's Time-of-Sale page lists the right numbers.

  • Assessing Division: 952-563-8722, for fees or fines associated with the property.
  • Utility Billing: 952-563-8726, for the current outstanding water bill.
  • Environmental Health: 952-563-8934, for pending civil fines.
  • Finance: 952-563-4527, for pending weeds, trees, brush removal and abatements.

Hennepin County bills the property tax, due May 15 and October 15, and it takes recordings by appointment, online through its Virtual Recorder site with a $3 service fee, by mail or through eRecording for title companies. Its recording page lists a $46 fee per document and a $54 well disclosure certificate when one is needed, and it says properties with delinquent taxes cannot be transferred under Minnesota Statute 272.12. Minnesota Statute 513.55 separately requires a written seller disclosure before the purchase agreement is signed.

faqs.q: Is the Bloomington inspection required for a cash sale?
faqs.a: Yes, it applies to any sale of a covered dwelling, cash or financed, listed or private. The only way out is one of the five exemptions in city code, and you still have to call the city to say which one applies.

faqs.q: Do I have to repair everything the Bloomington inspector finds?
faqs.a: No. Only the nine immediate hazard categories must be corrected, and the buyer can assume them with the city's written consent. Other deficiencies are listed in the report without a repair requirement.

faqs.q: How long is a Bloomington Time-of-Sale report valid?
faqs.a: One year from the date of issue, and only for the owner named on it.

faqs.q: Who gets the Certificate of Compliance?
faqs.a: The city sends it to the owner or listing agent once no hazards remain. It is typically required at closing, so ask your agent or title company to confirm they have it before the signing date.

faqs.q: Can an heir selling an inherited house in Bloomington skip the inspection?
faqs.a: Usually not. The sheriff and court-officer exemption does not apply to a sale by a person appointed by a probate court, so a personal representative should plan for the inspection and report.
